Learn · Chapter 11

Nervous communication

How does your body detect a change and respond?

Learning goal

I can explain how the nervous system detects changes and directs responses.

Before you begin

Start here: a stimulus is a change; a response is what the body does after that change.

How to complete this lesson — Learn → practise → required check → finish
  1. Start with the lesson. Read the learning goal and “Before you begin,” then work through the explanation, diagrams and examples below. The embedded textbook is optional support: open it when you want another explanation or a closer look at a figure.
  2. Use the learning goal and starting reminder. The learning goal above tells you what you must be able to explain. Read “Before you begin” next to connect this lesson to what you already know.
  3. Work through the online lesson in order. Read each teaching section and study its diagrams, examples and comparisons. Select an underlined biology term when you need its meaning. Use the video or Vocabulary help when an idea is still unclear.
  4. Complete the required written chapter check. Open the check near the bottom and select Start. This check contains written responses only; there is no multiple-choice question to unlock them. Answer each prompt in your own words and select Save written response for every response box.
  5. Submit only when the required work is complete. Check that every required item has been attempted and every written response is saved. Then select Submit and finish. This stops the timer, records the completed run in All My Work and updates chapter progress.
  6. Use optional practice only when it helps. Optional source practice and Practice & Review activities can help you study, but they do not count toward the 12 required chapter checks.

A cold hand gives us a starting point

You step outside without gloves. Your skin cools. A moment later, you pull your hands into your sleeves. Your body has detected a change, processed information about it, and produced a response. This chapter explains how those three jobs happen, from the whole nervous system down to the membrane of a single cell.

Start with this question: How can a change at one place in your body produce a useful response somewhere else? We will first follow the information, then examine the cells carrying it, and finally return to the brain and the systems they form.

Look at the middle box first. Integration means processing incoming information and organizing a response. The system cannot choose an appropriate response from an outgoing signal alone: information must first arrive. That is why sensory input comes before integration and motor output follows it.

Separate the change, the detector, and the response

A stimulus is a change that can be detected. A receptor detects it and starts sensory signalling. An effector, usually a muscle or gland, carries out the response. These names refer to different jobs. Cold is a stimulus; a temperature-sensitive receptor is a detector; contracting muscle is part of a response.

In the cold-hand example, receptors provide information about cooling. Processing in the CNS contributes to your decision to cover your hands. Motor signals reach skeletal muscles, which move your arms. The muscles do not need to understand the weather: they respond to the signals reaching them.

Worked example: why pulling on a sleeve is not just “a message from the brain”

  1. Identify what changed. Skin temperature fell. We start with the stimulus because the response needs a cause.
  2. Identify how the change becomes information. Temperature-sensitive receptors change their signalling. Without detection, the CNS would not receive this particular information.
  3. Locate processing. The CNS combines the sensory information with other information, including your awareness of being cold and your available choices.
  4. Follow output to an effector. Motor neurons carry signals to skeletal muscles. Their contraction moves the sleeves over your hands.
  5. Explain the result. Covering the hands reduces further heat loss. A complete answer connects the detected change to what the response accomplishes.

A reflex can use a much shorter processing route. Some other responses regulate organs without a conscious decision. Keep the three jobs in the model; do not assume that every response requires conscious thought.

Why communication matters for homeostasis

Your cells work within a limited range of conditions. Homeostasis is the maintenance of relatively stable internal conditions while the environment and your activities change. “Relatively stable” allows small fluctuations. It does not mean that temperature, heart rate, and every other variable stay at one exact value.

Consider cooling of the body, rather than just a decision about clothing. Temperature information reaches control centres that can increase heat conservation and heat production. Reduced blood flow near the skin reduces heat loss; shivering produces heat through muscle activity. These responses oppose the original fall in body temperature. As the disturbance decreases, the need for a strong corrective response also decreases. This is the reasoning behind negative feedback.

Nervous and endocrine communication help coordinate these adjustments. Neurons carry rapid electrical changes along their membranes and usually communicate chemically at junctions. Endocrine glands release hormones into blood; a hormone affects cells with suitable receptors. Nervous responses are generally rapid and targeted, while many hormonal effects develop more slowly and last longer. The two systems work together, and those timing descriptions are general patterns.

Not every nervous response is a negative-feedback loop. Choosing to wave to someone is nervous communication, but it does not necessarily correct a disturbed internal variable. When you call something homeostatic, identify the condition being regulated and explain how the response helps regulate it.

For warming, connect the response to heat loss: sweat glands release sweat onto the skin, and evaporation removes heat from the body. The gland is the effector, releasing sweat is its activity, and cooling is the effect that can oppose a temperature rise. Use those distinctions in the next example.

Try the roles: a warm room

A person enters a warm room and begins sweating. Identify a stimulus, a receptor's job, the processing job, an effector, and the response. Then explain how evaporation of sweat can oppose the temperature change.

Try it before opening the model. Compare your own reasoning; this response is not automatically marked or included in chapter progress.

Hint: an effector is a structure

“Sweating” names an activity. Which structure produces the sweat? Also separate detecting warmth from carrying out the cooling response.

Compare your explanation

A rise in body temperature is the disturbance. Temperature-sensitive receptors provide sensory information; CNS processing coordinates output to sweat glands. The glands release sweat, and evaporation removes heat from the body, opposing the rise. A strong answer names both the structures and the direction of the effect. If you wrote only “the brain makes you sweat,” add the input and explain why the output helps.

Place those jobs in the nervous system

The central nervous system (CNS) consists of the brain and spinal cord. The peripheral nervous system (PNS) connects them to the rest of the body. Sensory pathways carry information toward the CNS; motor pathways carry signals away to effectors. “Motor” means output, including output to glands and internal organs.

DivisionStructures or connectionsJob and example
CNSBrain and spinal cordProcesses information and organizes responses; includes spinal reflex circuits.
PNSNerves outside the brain and spinal cordConnects receptors and effectors with the CNS.
Somatic systemSomatic sensory pathways and motor pathways to skeletal muscleProvides body information and controls skeletal muscles, including voluntary movements and reflexes.
Autonomic systemMotor pathways to smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glandsRegulates activities such as heart rate and digestion without a conscious command.
Sympathetic divisionA division of autonomic outputHelps prepare the body for action; heart rate can increase while digestion slows.
Parasympathetic divisionA division of autonomic outputSupports functions such as digestion and slowing the heart during recovery.

You will use these divisions in detail later. For now, notice the nesting: sympathetic and parasympathetic are parts of autonomic control; they are not alternative names for the CNS and PNS.

A neuron is a cell; a nerve is a bundle

A neuron receives, conducts, and passes information. Many long nerve fibres are bundled with supporting tissue to make a nerve, much as many separate strands can share one cable. A single nerve can contain fibres carrying information in different directions. Glial cells support the working environment of neurons, provide nourishment and protection, and, in some cases, form insulation. They are active support cells, not spare neurons.

Apply the model to a new situation

You see a pencil rolling toward the edge of a desk and catch it. Explain the information pathway. Then judge this claim: “Every response controlled by the nervous system maintains homeostasis.” Use your example to support your judgement.

Try it before opening the model. Compare your own reasoning; this response is not automatically marked or included in chapter progress.

Optional hint: Separate information flow from regulation

Make a first attempt before using this hint. First trace what was detected, where it was processed and which structure moved. Then ask which internal condition, if any, the catch was correcting. A useful response is not automatically a homeostatic response.

Model and self-check

Visual receptors provide information about the moving pencil. Sensory pathways carry information to the CNS, where it is processed; somatic motor output reaches arm and hand muscles, which contract to catch the pencil. This action demonstrates nervous coordination but does not, by itself, identify an internal condition being kept stable. The claim is too broad. Check that you explained input, processing, output, and the limit of the homeostasis claim.

The Launch Lab on p. 365 explores how changing sensory information or hand movement affects a task. Before comparing completion times, ask whether a trial changed input, movement, or both. A slower time alone cannot tell you which part caused the difficulty.

Carry forward: a response requires a connected information pathway. Next we will examine the neuron, the cell that allows that pathway to carry a signal.

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

neuron
a nerve cell that receives and carries information
dendrite
a branch that receives information toward the cell body
axon
the extension that carries impulses away from the cell body
myelin

More vocabulary for this lesson

Lesson vocabulary

neuron · cell body · dendrite · axon · axon terminal · synapse · myelin · node of Ranvier · action potential · saltatory conduction · effector · CNS · PNS
Select an underlined term for its definition. Your vocabulary writing is saved in Process Collection.

How can one cell reach a distant muscle?

A nerve signal may need to travel from your spinal cord toward a muscle in your foot. A chain of round, identical cells would not explain the long fibres inside a nerve. Neurons have specialized shapes that let one cell receive many inputs and send information over a considerable distance.

Start with a typical multipolar neuron: it has many dendrites and one axon. Dendrites are branching receiving regions. The cell body, or soma, contains the nucleus and organelles and maintains the cell's metabolism. The axon carries action potentials toward its terminal branches. An action potential is a brief electrical change across a neuron’s membrane. Regenerating that change along the axon carries a nerve signal. For now, connect this signal with the continuous axon; Lessons 4 and 5 will explain the ion movements that produce it. An axon terminal passes a signal to another cell at a junction called a synapse.

Look first at the large yellow cell body on the left. Trace one short branch outward: that is a dendrite. Now follow the long yellow extension to the right under the blue coverings. That continuous extension is the axon; the blue coverings are insulation around it, not separate neurons. The large horizontal arrow means the usual direction of information flow through this model.

The narrowed region where the axon begins is labelled the axon hillock. Signals arriving at different receiving regions can combine and influence whether an action potential begins near the start of the axon. The cell body does not consciously choose. Its membranes respond to the combined electrical effects of incoming signals.

Finish at the terminal branches. Their branching allows the neuron to communicate with more than one target. The next cell is separated from a chemical synaptic terminal by a tiny synaptic cleft. The electrical signal along an axon and the chemical signal across that cleft are different parts of the pathway.

Use structure to explain function

Question: Why does a neuron benefit from having many short dendritic branches and one long axon? A useful answer must explain what the shape makes possible.

  1. Begin with reception. Many dendritic branches provide a large receiving surface. This allows many synaptic contacts rather than just one input.
  2. Connect reception to integration. Inputs influence the cell body and the region where the axon begins. Combining those effects allows the outgoing signal to depend on more than one incoming message.
  3. Connect length to distance. A long axon allows an action potential to reach a distant target while staying on one continuous cell membrane.
  4. Account for the ending. Terminal branches provide sites where the neuron can release chemical messengers to its target cells.

The conclusion is a structure–function explanation: branching supports receiving and distributing information; the long extension supports conduction over distance. Simply listing the four part names would leave that reasoning out.

The structure of a neuron: recap

As you watch: Pause at each labelled structure and explain its function without looking back at the table.

Load video Watch on YouTube

Video not playing? Use the written explanation on this page.

Follow through: cover the labels on the neuron image and draw its main outline. Add each label only after you can explain what that part contributes to communication. Include the continuous axon beneath the myelin.

Insulation changes how the impulse travels

The myelin sheath is a layered, fatty covering around many axons. It reduces electrical leakage through the covered membrane and helps a voltage change spread farther and faster along the axon. Gaps in the sheath are nodes of Ranvier. At these exposed regions, the membrane regenerates the action potential.

In the PNS, a Schwann cell wraps a segment of one axon to form myelin. In the CNS, oligodendrocytes form myelin. The glial-cell inset in the neuron image includes an oligodendrocyte; it is not a claim that Schwann cells make CNS myelin.

Compare the two panels from left to right. In the unmyelinated axon, neighbouring membrane regions regenerate the signal along the route. In the myelinated axon, the glowing gaps mark nodes where regeneration occurs. The curved arrows summarize movement of the signal between nodes. They do not show an ion jumping through the air or crossing a break in the axon.

This pattern is saltatory conduction. The word “jumping” describes where action potentials are regenerated. The underlying axon remains continuous, and local electrical current still travels through the regions under myelin. With other relevant conditions similar, myelin increases conduction speed. It does not make each action potential taller.

Compare the same featureMyelinated axonUnmyelinated axon
CoveringMyelin segments separated by nodesNo myelin sheath
Regeneration of the signalMainly at exposed nodesAlong neighbouring regions of axon membrane
ConductionFaster when other conditions are comparableSlower in that comparison
What stays continuousThe axon under the sheathThe axon along its length

Explain a diagram error

A student draws four separate short axons with empty spaces between them and says, “The impulse jumps across the empty spaces, so this is myelin.” Explain what must change in the drawing and why.

Try it before opening the model. Compare your own reasoning; this response is not automatically marked or included in chapter progress.

Hint: separate the axon from its covering

Where should a gap occur: in the neuron itself or in the insulation around it?

Compare your reasoning

Draw one continuous axon. Place separate myelin segments around it and label the exposed membrane between segments as nodes of Ranvier. Action potentials regenerate at the nodes while local current spreads along the intact axon. If the axon were actually disconnected, the diagram would not represent normal saltatory conduction.

Predicting the effect of damage

Suppose an axon is intact but part of its myelin is damaged. First identify what has been lost: insulation. More current can leak across the affected membrane. The next region may reach threshold—the level of electrical change needed to regenerate an action potential—later, or may fail to reach it. The result can be delayed or blocked signalling. The possible body effect depends on the pathway: a sensory pathway carries information toward the CNS; a motor pathway contributes to movement.

Multiple sclerosis (MS) involves immune-mediated damage in the CNS, including damage to myelin and sometimes axons. Depending on the affected pathways, symptoms may include altered sensation, visual problems, weakness, fatigue, or difficulties with coordination. The course differs among people. Myelin damage explains a mechanism for disrupted communication; it does not let us diagnose a person from a single symptom.

Do not use myelin alone to predict whether an injured neuron can regenerate. Recovery depends on the location and nature of the injury and its cellular environment. We will also distinguish grey and white matter later; grey matter is more than simply “neurons without myelin.”

Compare two different failures

In model A, a neuron's axon conducts normally, but its terminal cannot release a chemical messenger. In model B, a myelinated axon loses insulation along part of its length. Predict where communication could fail in each model. Would adding more dendritic branches necessarily repair either problem?

Try it before opening the model. Compare your own reasoning; this response is not automatically marked or included in chapter progress.

Optional hint: Locate each failure before proposing a repair

Make a first attempt before using this hint. Mark the conducting axon, the terminal and the receiving branches as different places. Ask which missing function additional input branches would actually restore.

Model and self-check

In A, the electrical signal reaches the terminal, but communication to the next cell fails at chemical release. In B, conduction toward the terminal may slow or fail because insulation is lost. More dendritic branches would provide more potential input sites; they would not directly restore terminal release machinery or the missing myelin. Check that you located two different failures and linked each prediction to the damaged structure.

Carry forward: a neuron's shape supports receiving, integrating, conducting, and passing information. Next we will connect several neurons into a pathway and explain why a withdrawal reflex can begin before conscious awareness.

Lesson vocabulary

stimulus · receptor · sensory neuron · interneuron · motor neuron · effector · response · reflex · reflex arc · neuron · cell body · CNS · claim
Select an underlined term for its definition. Your vocabulary writing is saved in Process Collection.

Why can your hand move before you decide to move it?

Imagine accidentally touching hot glassware. Your hand begins to withdraw before you have finished recognizing what happened. That order is possible because some processing occurs in a spinal circuit. The circuit can start motor output while information also travels toward brain regions involved in conscious perception.

Keep two questions separate: Which way does information travel? and Where is it processed? A sensory neuron is identified by its role in carrying information toward the CNS, not by whether you become conscious of that information immediately.

PartJobDirection or destination
Sensory receptorDetects a change and begins sensory signallingInformation enters a sensory pathway
Sensory (afferent) neuronCarries information from a receptorToward the CNS: afferent arrives
InterneuronProcesses or relays information between neuronsWithin the brain or spinal cord
Motor (efferent) neuronCarries output to an effectorAway from the CNS: efferent exits
EffectorChanges its activity in responseA muscle contracts or a gland secretes

The receptor and effector are the beginning and ending structures in this model. Sensory, inter-, and motor neurons connect them. Glial cells support the neurons' environment and conduction; they do not replace one of those three pathway roles.

Trace a withdrawal reflex, one connection at a time

Start at “stimulus,” beside the skin receptor. Follow the sensory route into the area marked spinal cord (CNS). The boundary matters: the sensory neuron brings information into the CNS, and an interneuron processes it there. Follow the motor route back out to the muscle. The separate upward path carries information toward the brain; it is not a detour that must finish before the muscle responds.

Worked explanation: withdrawal from a sharp object

  1. Detect the stimulus. A potentially damaging stimulus activates receptors in the skin. This starts sensory signalling rather than directly ordering the muscle to move.
  2. Carry the information inward. A sensory neuron conducts action potentials toward the spinal cord. The direction makes it afferent.
  3. Process within the spinal circuit. The sensory neuron communicates with interneurons that influence motor neurons. Several connections allow the response to coordinate muscles; the picture is a simplified account of that circuitry.
  4. Carry output outward. Motor neurons signal the skeletal muscles that withdraw the body part. Because their output goes to an effector, they are efferent.
  5. Explain the timing. This route does not wait for a conscious decision in the cerebrum. Information also ascends to the brain, allowing perception of the stimulus and further action.

A reflex is a rapid, involuntary response to a stimulus. A reflex arc is the neural route producing it. The response is the movement; the arc is the connected circuit. A spinal withdrawal reflex does not mean that the brain never receives information.

Reflex arcs: example 1

As you watch: Trace the sensory route into the CNS and the motor route to the effector. Distinguish the response from conscious awareness.

Load video Watch on YouTube

Video not playing? Use the written explanation on this page.

Follow through: redraw the two routes: one through the spinal circuit to the muscle, and one carrying information toward the brain. Explain why both routes can be active without waiting for a conscious decision.

Find the break in a pathway

In a simplified withdrawal circuit, the sensory neuron is unable to conduct, while the motor neuron and muscle remain functional. Would touching the receptor still initiate the usual withdrawal through this circuit? Explain the missing connection.

Try it before opening the model. Compare your own reasoning; this response is not automatically marked or included in chapter progress.

Hint: start at the receptor

An intact effector cannot act on information that never reaches the processing circuit. Trace the route in order.

Compare your reasoning

The receptor may detect the stimulus, but the sensory signal cannot reach the spinal circuit through the blocked neuron. The usual sensory input therefore does not activate the motor output through this route. An intact motor neuron and muscle could still respond to a different effective input; their being intact does not bypass the missing sensory link.

A deliberate response uses the same broad jobs

Now consider a driver who sees a cat move onto the road and deliberately presses the brake. Work through the response from the detected change to the foot movement. The response can be quick, but it is not the same circuit as withdrawing a hand from a sharp object.

  1. Detect the change. Visual receptors provide information about the cat on the road. This is sensory input, not yet the instruction to move a foot.
  2. Explain the processing. Brain circuits interpret the incoming information and contribute to selecting the braking response. This step connects seeing the obstacle with a deliberate action.
  3. Trace the outgoing route. Motor commands descend through pathways in the spinal cord and travel in motor neurons toward the leg and foot muscles. Using the brain does not mean bypassing the spinal cord.
  4. Identify the effector and result. Skeletal muscles contract so that the foot presses the brake. Naming the muscle’s role completes the connection between the detected change and the response.

The broad sequence is still input, integration, output. The important difference from the simplified spinal withdrawal example is the processing route that organizes the response. Do not say “a reflex uses the spinal cord but a voluntary movement does not.” A voluntary command from the brain can travel through the spinal cord on its way to an effector.

The main patellar, or knee-jerk, reflex is a useful contrast. Stretch receptors in a muscle detect stretching. A sensory neuron can synapse directly with the motor neuron that activates that same muscle. An interneuron is not needed in that particular connection, although interneurons help coordinate other muscles. Not every reflex arc has the identical five-box arrangement. Pupillary reflexes use brainstem circuits, so not every reflex is spinal either.

Video not playing? Use the written explanation on this page.

Follow through: identify the receptor, input neuron, processing connection, output neuron, and effector in the example you watch. If an interneuron is not shown, explain why that does not automatically make the pathway incorrect.

Shape and job answer different questions

Multipolar means many processes extend from the cell body: usually several dendrites and one axon. Bipolar means two main processes extend from it. In the common unipolar sensory arrangement taught here, one process leaves the cell body and branches into peripheral and central portions; it is often called pseudounipolar.

These describe shape. Sensory, interneuron, and motor describe function. You cannot classify a cell as “motor” merely because it is long, or decide that every drawing must look like the multipolar neuron in Lesson 2. Find the direction of information and the structures it connects.

Two observations, two routes

A person withdraws a foot from an unexpectedly sharp surface, then looks down and deliberately steps around it. Explain the first and second responses using sensory input, processing location, motor output, and effector. Why does the first response not show that the brain was disconnected?

Try it before opening the model. Compare your own reasoning; this response is not automatically marked or included in chapter progress.

Optional hint: Keep the first response separate from the later choice

Make a first attempt before using this hint. Follow the first route to a muscle, then follow the information that permits awareness and a planned step. A short route need not prevent a longer route from also carrying information.

Model and self-check

The sharp stimulus activates a sensory pathway to the spinal cord, where a withdrawal circuit can activate motor neurons to the leg muscles. Information also travels toward the brain. Looking and deliberately stepping around the object involve further sensory input and brain processing; commands can descend through the spinal cord to somatic motor neurons and skeletal muscles. The earlier movement indicates that a spinal response began without waiting for conscious processing, not that no information reached the brain. Include the direction of both sensory and motor signals.

Optional investigation: make a fair comparison

Investigation 11.A, p. 371 compares reflex responses. Before an observation, name the stimulus, predicted response, and variable you will record. Use the same observation method across trials, repeat observations, and distinguish “a response occurred” from “this circuit has been proven.” Follow your teacher's procedure for any physical test.

For example, repeated pupil-size observations under two ordinary room-light conditions could test whether the visible response changes with light level. Keep observation distance and the time allowed for adjustment consistent. A pupil becoming smaller is the observation; activity in a particular neural route is the explanation supported by your biology model.

Carry forward: we can now trace a pathway. Next we will explain what changes within a neuron's membrane so that it can carry an electrical signal at all.

Planning a fair comparison is not the same as collecting data. No reflex measurements are supplied here. Any physical investigation must follow the procedure and safety conditions your teacher has approved; do not create painful stimuli, throw objects at someone’s eyes, or use bright lights to improvise a test.

The resting neuron

What is happening at the membrane before a neuron fires?

Learning goal

Chapter 11 · pp. 374–375

Open at p. 374

Key terms: resting membrane potential · Na⁺ · K⁺ · potassium leak channel · sodium-potassium pump · selective permeability

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

resting membrane potential
the voltage difference across a resting neuron’s membrane
selective permeability
allowing some substances across a membrane more easily than others
depolarization
the inside of the membrane becoming less negative
repolarization
the membrane voltage returning toward its resting level
More vocabulary for this lesson

Lesson vocabulary

resting membrane potential · ion gradient · selective permeability · axon · neuron · depolarization · repolarization · refractory period
Select an underlined term for its definition. Your vocabulary writing is saved in Process Collection.

A resting neuron is ready, not switched off

A neuron can send a signal within milliseconds, but it cannot create the conditions for that signal from nothing. Before an impulse begins, its membrane already separates different ion concentrations and a small amount of electrical charge. This stored electrochemical difference makes a rapid response possible.

Picture a very small patch of axon membrane. There is fluid on the inside and fluid on the outside. An ion is a charged particle: sodium, Na⁺, and potassium, K⁺, each carry one positive charge. Large negatively charged molecules are also present inside. Both positive and negative particles occur on both sides; the important voltage difference comes from a small imbalance near the membrane.

The membrane is a boundary. Its lipid interior prevents ions from passing freely, while specific proteins provide routes across. That selective permeability lets the cell maintain different conditions on its two sides.

What does −70 mV actually say?

Membrane potential is the voltage inside relative to outside. We use the outside as our reference. A reading of −70 mV means that the inside is 70 millivolts lower in electrical potential than the outside. It does not mean there are no positive ions inside, or that the entire cell is filled with a large net negative charge.

A typical example of a resting membrane potential is −70 mV. Actual values vary among cells. “Resting” means the membrane is not producing an action potential at that time. Ions still move through channels, and the cell still uses ATP, a molecule that transfers energy for cellular work such as active transport.

Worked example: read a change before naming it

A recording changes from −70 mV to −60 mV. Has the inside become more negative or less negative?

  1. Keep the reference fixed. Both readings describe inside relative to outside.
  2. Compare the values. −60 is higher than −70, so the voltage rose by 10 mV.
  3. Interpret the sign. The inside is still negative relative to outside, but it is less negative than before.
  4. Name the change. Becoming less negative is depolarization. It does not yet tell us whether an action potential occurred; we need the threshold and subsequent events.

From −70 mV to −80 mV would be the opposite: the inside becomes more negative. Read the numbers before using words such as “higher,” “lower,” or “more charged.”

Three connected conditions produce the resting state

First, ions are distributed unequally. There is a higher concentration of Na⁺ outside the neuron and a higher concentration of K⁺ inside. A concentration gradient is a difference in concentration between places. If a suitable route is open, that difference tends to drive net movement from higher toward lower concentration.

Second, the resting membrane is more permeable to K⁺ than to Na⁺. Potassium can leave through leak channels more readily than sodium can enter. When positive K⁺ leaves, the inside becomes more negative relative to outside. The increasingly negative interior attracts positive ions back, opposing further net K⁺ loss. This electrical influence and the concentration difference act together; ions do not respond to concentration alone. Large negatively charged molecules that cannot leave also contribute to the conditions inside.

Third, active transport maintains the gradients. The sodium–potassium pump uses ATP to move 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in per cycle. These movements are against their concentration gradients. The pump continually offsets leakage and the ion movements associated with signalling, keeping the cell ready over time.

Start with the membrane running horizontally across the picture. Above it is extracellular fluid; below it is intracellular fluid. Orange Na⁺ symbols are more common outside and purple K⁺ symbols are more common inside. The symbols show relative concentrations, not a literal count of all the ions in a cell.

Now read each arrow separately. The sodium leak arrow points inward; the potassium leak arrow points outward. These channels allow passive movement. At the larger pump, three Na⁺ arrows point out while two K⁺ arrows point in. That protein uses ATP. The −70 mV label describes the resulting electrical state; it is not the voltage of an individual ion.

The distinction to keep: channels provide routes for ions to move down electrochemical gradients; the pump uses energy to maintain concentration gradients. The resting membrane's greater permeability to K⁺ is a major immediate contributor to resting voltage. The pump is essential, but its 3-to-2 exchange alone is not the whole explanation.

Account for one pump cycle

For one sodium–potassium pump cycle, state the movement of each ion, the energy requirement, and the net direction of positive charge. Then explain why this calculation does not, by itself, explain the entire resting potential.

Try it before opening the model. Compare your own reasoning; this response is not automatically marked or included in chapter progress.

Hint: count charges, then consider other routes

Na⁺ and K⁺ both have one positive charge. Compare three positive charges leaving with two entering. What else crosses the membrane through channels?

Compare your reasoning

The pump moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in using ATP. This is a net transfer of one positive charge outward per cycle. However, ions also move passively through channels, especially K⁺ through resting leak channels. Resting voltage depends on the gradients, selective permeability, and electrical forces as well as active transport. Include both the arithmetic and the limitation.

What would happen if ATP became unavailable?

Separate an immediate event from a longer-term effect. If pumping stops, the existing gradients do not disappear at the same instant. There are still different ion concentrations, and ions can still move through channels. As movement continues without active maintenance, the gradients become harder to sustain, and normal signalling eventually fails.

This explains why “resting” tissue still needs a supply of energy. Maintaining readiness is work. It also prepares us for the next lesson: the rapid upward and downward changes during an action potential are caused mainly by changes in channel permeability, not by a pump suddenly turning on and off.

Electrical conduction: overview

As you watch: Identify the resting state before the voltage changes. Keep ion movement separate from the voltage it produces.

Predict from a changed condition

In a classroom membrane model, more K⁺ channels open while the initial ion gradients are unchanged. For this first moment, assume the net movement through them is K⁺ leaving the cell. Predict the direction of the voltage change and explain it. Would “K⁺ is positive, so the inside must become more positive” be sound reasoning?

Try it before opening the model. Compare your own reasoning; this response is not automatically marked or included in chapter progress.

Optional hint: Track charge across the boundary

Make a first attempt before using this hint. Count the sign of the charge and the direction it moves. Use only the initial conditions specified; do not assume the same net movement continues indefinitely.

Model and self-check

Positive charge leaving tends to make the inside more negative relative to outside. The claim ignores the direction of movement: a positive ion entering and the same ion leaving have opposite effects. The model specifies net outward movement at that moment; it does not predict an unlimited fall in voltage because electrical forces and gradients change as ions move. Check that you used both charge and direction.

Optional model investigation

Investigation 11.B, p. 375 uses solutions separated by dialysis tubing to explore a voltage difference. The tubing models a boundary; the solutions model different ion environments. It does not contain a neuron's full set of selective channels or an ATP-driven pump. A changing voltage in that model cannot demonstrate every mechanism of a living neuron.

Carry forward: the resting membrane is prepared by gradients and selective permeability. Next we will change the permeability and follow the resulting action potential.

Chapter 11 · pp. 377–380

Open at p. 377

Key terms: action potential · threshold · depolarization · repolarization · hyperpolarization · refractory period

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

action potential
a rapid, all-or-none change in membrane voltage
threshold
the voltage at which an action potential starts
refractory period
a recovery time that limits how soon a neuron can fire again
saltatory conduction
conduction in which the impulse is regenerated at the nodes of a myelinated axon
More vocabulary for this lesson

Lesson vocabulary

action potential · threshold · depolarization · repolarization · hyperpolarization · refractory period · absolute refractory period · relative refractory period · channel inactivation · propagation · stimulus · neuron · axon · motor neuron · myelin · node of Ranvier · saltatory conduction · mechanism
Select an underlined term for its definition. Your vocabulary writing is saved in Process Collection.

How can a brief voltage change travel a long distance?

A resting axon has more Na⁺ outside, more K⁺ inside, and a membrane potential often represented as −70 mV. The next step is a temporary change in the membrane's permeability. An action potential is a rapid sequence of voltage changes produced by controlled ion movement through membrane channels.

We will first study one small region of membrane over time. Only after that will we follow the signal along the axon. A graph showing one region changing with time is not a picture of sodium ions travelling from the cell body to a muscle.

Reaching threshold starts a self-reinforcing rise

Incoming stimulation can make the inside less negative: the membrane depolarizes. Some changes are too small to initiate an action potential. In our common example, the membrane must reach a threshold near −55 mV at the trigger region.

At threshold, enough voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are activated for Na⁺ entry to produce further depolarization, which opens more Na⁺ channels. This self-reinforcing process produces the rapid rising phase. Na⁺ is driven inward by its electrochemical gradient; bringing positive charge in makes the inside more positive relative to outside.

Depolarization and an action potential are not synonyms. A small change from −70 to −65 mV is depolarization, but it does not reach a −55 mV threshold. An action potential is the full triggered event, including its rise and recovery. “No action potential” does not mean “no membrane change at all.”

Read the graph as a sequence of causes

In panel A, the horizontal axis is time in milliseconds and the vertical axis is membrane potential in millivolts. The resting line is about −70 mV and the dashed threshold line is about −55 mV. The peak in this illustration is labelled about +30 mV. Other examples may use +35 or +40 mV; these are representative values, not a different underlying process.

Read the rising section before the falling section. The lower panels show the associated membrane events. Their arrows show ions crossing a small membrane patch. They do not show the direction that the whole impulse travels along an axon.

  1. Resting state: the gradients are already present. Voltage-gated channels are not producing an action potential, although leak channels and pumps continue working.
  2. Rapid depolarization: Na⁺ permeability rises as voltage-gated sodium channels open. Na⁺ enters, making the inside less negative and then positive relative to outside.
  3. The rise stops: sodium channels become inactivated. Their temporary inability to conduct is different from simply being closed and ready to open. Delayed opening of voltage-gated K⁺ channels also changes the balance of current.
  4. Repolarization: K⁺ moves outward through those channels. Positive charge leaves, so the membrane potential falls toward its resting value.
  5. Hyperpolarization: some K⁺ channels remain open briefly, allowing an undershoot below the resting potential. As they close and normal resting conductances dominate again, the voltage returns toward resting level.

The sodium–potassium pump maintains the ion gradients over time. It is not the main mechanism producing the rapid falling phase. Also, only a small fraction of the available ions crosses during an ordinary action potential: the voltage reverses, but the overall Na⁺ and K⁺ concentration gradients do not exchange sides.

Worked example: name the event from the evidence

A membrane record starts at −70 mV, rises through −55 mV, peaks above zero, falls, and briefly reaches −80 mV. At the falling part of the curve, what movement of ions best explains the change?

  1. Locate the phase. We are after the peak and moving toward a more negative inside voltage.
  2. Choose a charge movement that fits. Positive charge leaving the cell would lower its inside voltage.
  3. Match that movement to the channel sequence. Voltage-gated K⁺ channels are open and K⁺ moves out; Na⁺ channels are inactivated.
  4. Interpret the undershoot separately. Continued K⁺ permeability briefly takes the voltage below the usual resting level. That is hyperpolarization, not a second action potential.

If you had answered “the pump pushes all the sodium back out,” you would have confused gradual maintenance of gradients with the fast channel events on the graph.

Does each change trigger an action potential?

Use a threshold of −55 mV. In three separate trials, a neuron's trigger region depolarizes from −70 mV to −62 mV, to −57 mV, and then to threshold. Identify which trials show depolarization and which can initiate an action potential, assuming the membrane is ready to fire.

Try it before opening the model. Compare your own reasoning; this response is not automatically marked or included in chapter progress.

Hint: compare every value with both starting voltage and threshold

A voltage can move toward threshold without reaching it. The third trial explicitly reaches the required level.

Compare your reasoning

All three trials involve depolarization because the inside becomes less negative. The first two remain below the −55 mV threshold and do not initiate an action potential in this model. The third reaches threshold and triggers the event. A complete answer separates a graded change in voltage from the all-or-none action potential.

The three trials above are model conditions for reasoning, not reported measurements from an experiment.

Recovery makes another immediate impulse impossible

During the absolute refractory period, the affected membrane region cannot generate another action potential, even with a stronger stimulus. Many sodium channels are inactivated and must recover before they can participate again.

During the later relative refractory period, some channels have recovered, but a stronger-than-usual stimulus is needed. Continuing K⁺ conductance and the more negative voltage can make reaching threshold harder. These periods overlap the later phases of the voltage event; recovery is not simply a switch that flips when the graph first touches −70 mV.

The refractory period limits how closely action potentials can follow one another. It also helps explain normal forward propagation. Local current from an active region can spread in both directions, but the region just behind the travelling impulse is recovering. The ready region ahead can reach threshold and regenerate the signal.

Regeneration keeps the signal from fading

In an unmyelinated axon, depolarization at one region produces local current that brings the next region to threshold. The next region then generates its own action potential. The signal is repeatedly renewed; one weak voltage change is not simply drifting all the way to the terminal.

In a myelinated axon, current spreads along the axon under the insulation and the next node regenerates the action potential. Return to the myelin comparison if needed: the axon is continuous, but its exposed regeneration sites are spaced apart. Sodium ions are not required to travel the entire length of the axon.

Normal impulses initiated near an axon's beginning travel toward its terminals. If an experiment stimulates an otherwise resting axon in its middle, both neighbouring directions can initially contain ready membrane. The usual one-way result depends on where an impulse starts and which regions are refractory; it is not an absolute rule that local electrical current can only move in one direction.

Action potential recap 1

As you watch: Track which ion moves, which direction it moves, and what happens to the inside voltage.

Load video Watch on YouTube

Video not playing? Use the written explanation on this page.

Follow through: point to a rising and a falling region of the graph and name the ion, its direction, and the resulting voltage change. Keep that across-membrane movement separate from propagation along the axon.

A stronger stimulus changes firing patterns, not spike height

All-or-none means that a ready membrane produces a full action potential once threshold is reached. Under the same conditions, a stronger stimulus does not make that neuron's individual spikes proportionally taller. An intense stimulus can instead increase firing frequency and recruit more neurons.

Compare equal lengths of time in the two rows. The heights remain the same, but the lower row contains more spikes. That is increased frequency. Recruitment would require evidence that additional neurons are active; you cannot infer it just by counting spikes from one neuron.

Worked comparison: two recordings from the same neuron

Use these supplied teaching-model numbers, not experimental measurements. Suppose one 100 ms interval contains 2 spikes and another contains 5. Because 100 ms is 0.10 s, the frequencies are 2 ÷ 0.10 = 20 impulses/s and 5 ÷ 0.10 = 50 impulses/s. If the spike heights are unchanged, the evidence supports a frequency increase. It does not show that each impulse became stronger, or that more neurons fired.

In a whole muscle, recruiting more motor units (motor neurons together with the muscle fibres they control) and increasing firing frequency can increase force. In a simplified experiment with one motor neuron, a fixed muscle preparation, one isolated pulse per trial, and recovery between trials, an above-threshold pulse does not become a larger neuronal action potential when its stimulus voltage is increased. Always identify what the experiment holds constant.

Carry forward: changing channel permeability produces a travelling series of regenerated action potentials. When the signal reaches the terminal, there is a new problem: the next cell is separated by a gap. Lesson 6 explains how chemical communication crosses it.

Key terms: synapse · presynaptic · postsynaptic · neurotransmitter · excitatory · inhibitory · summation

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

synapse
a junction where a neuron communicates with another cell
neurotransmitter
a chemical messenger released by the sending neuron
acetylcholine
a neurotransmitter that stimulates skeletal muscle and is also used in other pathways
reuptake
taking a released neurotransmitter back into a cell
More vocabulary for this lesson

Lesson vocabulary

synapse · neurotransmitter · acetylcholine · cholinesterase · reuptake · norepinephrine · action potential · axon · axon terminal · neuron · motor neuron · receptor · response · threshold · CNS · PNS · epinephrine
Select an underlined term for its definition. Your vocabulary writing is saved in Process Collection.

The electrical signal reaches a gap

An action potential can travel along one continuous axon membrane. At a chemical synapse, however, the sending and receiving cells have separate membranes. The action potential does not simply leap across the fluid-filled gap. The sending neuron converts its arriving electrical event into release of a chemical messenger.

The sending side is presynaptic; the receiving side is postsynaptic. The junction is the synapse, and the gap itself is the synaptic cleft. The messenger is a neurotransmitter. A synapse from a motor neuron to a muscle fibre is a neuromuscular junction.

Think of three connected events: an electrical signal arrives, a chemical messenger crosses the cleft, and the receiving cell's activity changes. The cells do not share one action potential. A new one can be generated in the receiving cell if the conditions for it are met.

Follow release, diffusion, binding, and clearance

Begin at the axon entering the top of panel A. The large arrow follows the arriving action potential toward the terminal. The terminal boundary separates the presynaptic cytoplasm from the cleft. The boundary below the gap belongs to the receiving cell. Small messenger dots cross the gap; the vesicles that held them do not travel into the next cell.

  1. The action potential depolarizes the terminal. This voltage change opens voltage-gated calcium channels there. Na⁺ dominated the rising phase along the axon; Ca²⁺ has a different job at release.
  2. Ca²⁺ enters the terminal. Its entry triggers synaptic vesicles to fuse with the presynaptic membrane.
  3. Vesicles release neurotransmitter by exocytosis. Fusion opens the vesicle to the cleft, so its chemical contents are released outside the sending cell.
  4. Neurotransmitter diffuses across the cleft. Molecules move through the fluid to the receiving membrane.
  5. Binding changes the receiving cell's activity. A messenger binds a suitable receptor. This can change ion-channel activity directly or through processes inside the cell. The resulting postsynaptic effect may promote or oppose firing.
  6. The signal is cleared. Neurotransmitter can be removed by reuptake, enzymatic breakdown, or diffusion away. Clearance lets signalling end and allows later messages to remain distinct.

The blue channels at the bottom of panel A represent receptor-linked ion pathways. The final large arrow is a possible continuation, if threshold is reached. One arriving input does not guarantee a new action potential.

Panel B ends on a muscle fibre rather than another neuron. The axon terminal releases acetylcholine onto the muscle membrane. Activation of the muscle's receptors depolarizes it and normally initiates the events leading to contraction. The pink receiving structure is an effector, not a dendrite.

The messenger and the enzyme have different jobs

Acetylcholine (ACh) is a neurotransmitter. At the skeletal neuromuscular junction, it activates receptors that allow a depolarizing membrane response and normally trigger muscle excitation. Cholinesterase—specifically acetylcholinesterase at this junction—is an enzyme that breaks down ACh. It helps end the message.

These are not two opposing neurotransmitters. One carries a signal; the other catalyzes its breakdown. For ACh, breakdown products can be taken up and reused. For transmitters such as norepinephrine and dopamine, reuptake of the transmitter itself is an important removal mechanism. Do not assume that every transmitter is cleared in exactly the same way.

Worked example: an impulse arrives but no message is released

Suppose the action potential reaches a terminal normally, but its voltage-gated calcium channels cannot open. Predict what happens next.

  1. Keep the successful event. Conduction along the axon occurred; there is no evidence of a failure there.
  2. Locate the blocked event. Without the normal Ca²⁺ entry, the usual trigger for vesicle fusion is missing.
  3. Follow the consequence across the gap. Much less, or no evoked, transmitter is released, so the postsynaptic receptors do not receive the usual chemical signal.
  4. Limit the conclusion. The receiving cell might still respond to a different input. This result concerns communication through the affected terminal.

Which side changed?

A transmitter is present in the cleft, but the receiving cell has no functioning receptors for it. Explain why the signal can fail even though release and diffusion worked.

Try it before opening the model. Compare your own reasoning; this response is not automatically marked or included in chapter progress.

Hint: arrival is not activation

Which event connects a molecule in the cleft to a change in ion movement across the receiving membrane?

Compare your reasoning

Transmitter must bind a suitable functioning receptor to produce its usual postsynaptic effect. Without that receptor response, the presence of transmitter does not cause the normal change in channels or receiving-cell activity. The failure is on the receiving side, unlike blocked Ca²⁺ entry or failed vesicle release on the sending side.

Inputs can move a neuron toward or away from firing

An excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) makes an action potential more likely. In a common example, channels allow a net inward movement of positive charge, producing a small depolarization toward threshold. An inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP) makes firing less likely. In the simple examples used here, K⁺ leaves or Cl⁻ enters, making the inside more negative.

The effect depends on the receiving membrane and its receptors. “Excitatory” and “inhibitory” describe effects at a particular synapse. They are not permanent labels that explain every action of a transmitter throughout the body. Inhibition can also work without a large visible hyperpolarization, by reducing the effect of excitatory current.

Compare A and B first. The small curves are local postsynaptic voltage changes, not full axonal action potentials. Their direction illustrates excitation or inhibition. A local rise in a dendrite does not by itself establish that the axon's trigger region has reached threshold. Now move to panel C: several inputs influence the combined effect near the start of the axon.

Summation asks what the inputs do together

Spatial summation combines inputs from different synapses close enough in time for their effects to overlap. Temporal summation combines repeated input from a synapse before the earlier effects have faded. In each case, the net effect at the trigger region determines whether threshold is reached.

On the left, several input routes converge: that spatial arrangement represents different presynaptic sources. On the right, closely repeated inputs represent a timing effect. The converging arrows do not mean that action potentials merge into a larger spike. Postsynaptic effects combine; the resulting axonal action potential remains all-or-none.

Worked model: include inhibition in the calculation

Use a simplified additive model at the trigger region. Resting voltage is −70 mV, threshold is −55 mV, and simultaneous contributions are +8 mV, +9 mV, and −5 mV.

  1. Add all contributions. +8 + 9 − 5 = +12 mV. Leaving out the inhibitory term would overestimate the net depolarization.
  2. Apply the net change to the starting value. −70 + 12 = −58 mV.
  3. Compare with threshold. −58 is still below −55, so no action potential is initiated in this model.
  4. Test the changed condition. Removing the −5 mV input would give a predicted depolarization to −53 mV, which crosses threshold and triggers an action potential. −53 mV is the model's threshold-crossing prediction, not the voltage at which the neuron would remain afterward.

Real synapses interact in more complex ways than simple addition. The calculation is a model for reasoning about combined effects, timing, and threshold; it is not a universal equation for a real neuron.

Learn the chemical names with a useful example

ChemicalExample roleWhat to remember
AcetylcholineExcites skeletal muscle at the neuromuscular junction; also used in CNS and autonomic pathwaysA messenger whose effect depends on the receptor. It can help slow the heart in a different pathway.
CholinesteraseBreaks down acetylcholineAn enzyme that helps terminate a signal, not a neurotransmitter.
NorepinephrineUsed in CNS signalling and by many sympathetic neuronsConnect it with alertness and sympathetic responses; the specific target determines the effect.
GABAA major inhibitory transmitter in the mature CNSOften reduces the likelihood of firing through receptor-dependent effects on ion movement.
DopamineContributes to movement control and reward-related learningIt is not a universal “excitatory chemical” or a complete explanation of pleasure or addiction.
SerotoninContributes to regulation of mood, sleep, and other functionsIts effects vary across receptors and circuits.
Glutamate and endorphinsGlutamate commonly supports excitation; endorphins help modulate pain signallingUse the role in the specific pathway rather than treating the name as a complete mechanism.

Give particular attention to acetylcholine, norepinephrine, and cholinesterase, and be able to use GABA in an inhibitory example. Epinephrine can act as a chemical signal too; when the adrenal medulla releases it into blood, it is functioning as a hormone.

Excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters

As you watch: Compare the effect on the postsynaptic membrane rather than memorizing only the transmitter’s name.

Load video Watch on YouTube

Video not playing? Use the written explanation on this page.

Follow through: explain an excitatory and an inhibitory example by stating the ion movement and effect on firing. Do not stop at the transmitter's name.

Explain a timing experiment

In this model experiment, one small input produces a depolarization that stays below threshold. The same synapse is activated repeatedly, close together in time, and an action potential occurs. When the activations are far apart, it does not occur. Name the type of summation and explain all three observations. Would the successful trial require a taller action potential?

Try it before opening the model. Compare your own reasoning; this response is not automatically marked or included in chapter progress.

Optional hint: Ask what can overlap in time

Make a first attempt before using this hint. Compare how much of an earlier postsynaptic effect remains when the next input arrives. Then keep the threshold decision separate from the height of the resulting spike.

Model and self-check

This is temporal summation. One input is insufficient. Closely spaced inputs arrive before earlier effects have faded, so the combined depolarization can reach threshold. Widely spaced inputs fade between activations and do not accumulate sufficiently. Reaching threshold triggers an ordinary all-or-none action potential; summation changes the likelihood of firing, not its height. Include timing and threshold in your explanation.

Optional tissue investigation

Investigation 11.C, p. 381 compares neural tissue and neuromuscular junctions. In a sketch, distinguish a motor neuron's axon terminal from the muscle membrane it contacts. A tissue image shows structural relationships; a still image alone cannot demonstrate the complete release sequence.

Carry forward: each synaptic step has a specific job. We can now predict what happens when a drug changes one of those steps.

You may analyse the textbook’s supplied micrographs and label features that are actually visible. That is image interpretation, not a claim that you used a microscope. Handling slides and equipment belongs to a separate teacher-approved practical activity; do not invent observations from missing specimens.

Key terms

More vocabulary for this lesson

Lesson vocabulary

synapse · neurotransmitter · receptor · agonist · antagonist · reuptake · acetylcholine · cholinesterase · mechanism
Select an underlined term for its definition. Your vocabulary writing is saved in Process Collection.

A changed synapse is a test of the normal one

If a drug changes behaviour or movement, “it affects the brain” is only a starting statement. A biological explanation identifies what step changes, how signalling changes, and what the affected pathway normally does. The same increase in chemical signalling can have different effects in an excitatory and an inhibitory pathway.

Reconstruct the normal sequence first: transmitter is synthesized and stored; an action potential and Ca²⁺ entry trigger release; transmitter diffuses across the cleft and binds receptors; it is then cleared. A drug may alter any of these steps, or affect conduction along the axon before the signal even reaches a synapse.

Read the four numbered locations as possible sites of a change. The line through them organizes the order of events, not the physical length of an axon. Locate a drug's action in that sequence before predicting whether the target cell receives more activation, less activation, or a longer-lasting signal.

Different mechanisms can produce similar-looking effects

Changed stepPossible mechanismFirst consequence to explain
Synthesis or storageLess transmitter is made or stored in vesiclesLess may be available for later release.
ReleaseRelease is increased or vesicle fusion is blockedMore or less transmitter reaches the cleft.
Receptor activationAn agonist activates a receptor; an antagonist blocks activationThe receiving cell responds differently even if normal transmitter release continues.
ClearanceReuptake or breakdown is slowed; breakdown is increasedThe chemical signal may last longer or be shortened.

An agonist activates a receptor. An antagonist prevents its normal activation. A reuptake blocker need not activate the receptor itself: it can increase the time released transmitter remains available. These mechanisms should not be treated as interchangeable.

Stimulant and depressant describe broad effects on nervous-system activity. A depressant is not simply a substance that makes someone feel sad. Nor does every receptor blocker depress the whole nervous system: blocking an inhibitory input can make a receiving neuron more likely to fire. Always establish what the affected pathway normally does.

Worked example: slow the removal of dopamine

Cocaine can block dopamine reuptake into the presynaptic neuron. Explain how that changes communication, without saying that it creates an extra-tall action potential.

  1. Name the normal process. Released dopamine binds receptors and is normally cleared partly by transporters that take it back up.
  2. Locate the change. Reuptake is blocked. This changes clearance, not the initial size of the action potential in the axon.
  3. Predict the immediate consequence. Dopamine remains available in the cleft longer and can continue influencing its receptors.
  4. Connect to the circuit. Dopamine participates in reward-related learning as well as other functions. Altered signalling can strongly reinforce behaviour, but the chemical name alone does not explain every effect of the drug.
  5. Limit the inference. A mechanism for reinforcement is not proof that every person develops addiction after one exposure. A hypothesis about a possible pathway needs evidence about repeated behaviour and other influences.

This is how to handle an explanation question: follow the normal step, change that step, then follow the consequences. Keep broader claims proportional to the evidence.

Contrast two ways to disrupt acetylcholine signalling

Botulinum toxin reduces acetylcholine release at peripheral cholinergic terminals, including skeletal neuromuscular junctions. The action potential may arrive, but the normal release process fails. The muscle receives less excitation and can become weak or paralyzed. This is a problem on the sending side; it is not best explained as toxin occupying the muscle's ACh receptor.

Sarin and some insecticides inhibit acetylcholinesterase activity. ACh is not broken down normally, so stimulation can persist. Excessive cholinergic activation disrupts normal coordinated function and can ultimately produce weakness or paralysis as well as initial excessive activity. Similar severe outcomes do not establish that two substances act by the same mechanism.

Worked reasoning: release failure means less ACh arrives at receptors. Breakdown failure means ACh remains available longer after it arrives. Both disturb normal movement, but one reduces the usual message while the other prevents it ending normally. A useful comparison names that difference before naming an outcome.

Predict a receiving-side block

A model substance prevents ACh from activating receptors on skeletal muscle. ACh release and breakdown are unchanged. Predict the effect on muscle excitation and compare it with a substance that blocks ACh release.

Try it before opening the model. Compare your own reasoning; this response is not automatically marked or included in chapter progress.

Hint: follow the messenger to its target

Does the first substance prevent ACh from reaching the cleft, or prevent the muscle from responding to it?

Compare your reasoning

The first substance reduces the muscle's response by blocking receptor activation on the receiving side. The second reduces the amount of ACh released from the sending side. Both can reduce muscle excitation, but ACh can still be present in the cleft with the receptor blocker. Check that your explanation distinguishes a similar effect from the different steps producing it.

A drug can also affect the signal before the synapse

Local anaesthetics provide a useful comparison: they can block voltage-gated sodium channels, preventing normal action-potential conduction along affected axons. With insufficient Na⁺ entry, the next section does not undergo the normal regenerative depolarization. A signal may therefore fail to reach a terminal even if the terminal's vesicles and the receiving cell's receptors are intact.

Nicotine, in contrast, activates certain acetylcholine receptors. Caffeine is a familiar stimulant that blocks adenosine receptors, reducing some signalling that normally promotes sleepiness. These examples show why “all stimulants release more transmitter” is too simple. You are not expected to infer a substance's exact action from its category or from a person's appearance.

Use an experiment to distinguish two hypotheses

In a classroom model, a substance weakens transmission from neuron A to neuron B. Recording shows normal action potentials arriving at A's terminal. Applying the usual transmitter directly to B produces a normal response. Compare these hypotheses: (1) the substance blocks conduction along A's axon; (2) it reduces transmitter release from A. Which better fits the observations, and what would you measure next?

Try it before opening the model. Compare your own reasoning; this response is not automatically marked or included in chapter progress.

Optional hint: Use the controls to eliminate a proposed failure

Make a first attempt before using this hint. A normal signal at A’s terminal checks one part of the route. A normal response to transmitter placed at B checks another. Identify what has not yet been measured directly.

Model and self-check

Normal arrival of action potentials argues against a conduction block in the tested axon. B's response to directly applied transmitter indicates that its receptors and response mechanism can still work. Reduced release is therefore the better of these two explanations. Measuring transmitter release or terminal Ca²⁺ entry would test the proposed failure more directly. These observations do not prove a unique molecular target: several presynaptic processes could reduce release. A strong answer uses both observations and states that limit.

One last comparison: what if the normal input is inhibitory?

Imagine a neuron receiving an inhibitory GABA input and several excitatory inputs. Reducing the inhibitory receptor response removes some opposition to firing. The neuron may now reach threshold more readily. This is disinhibition. It explains why a statement such as “a blocker always lowers nervous activity” is unreliable without identifying the target.

For the optional Thought Lab 11.1, p. 383, build your explanation around one mechanism, its predicted effect, and evidence that could test it. Broader addiction questions can also be explored in the optional extension. No personal experience is needed for either task.

Carry forward: we can predict how cells communicate and how that communication fails. Next we will organize those cells into the peripheral pathways that control different effectors.
